content: Chlorhexidine-containing skin disinfection preparations, when compared to non-chlorhexidine-containing products, were found to reduce the risk of local infections and phlebitis in adults, adolescents, children, and neonates. However, no significant difference was observed in catheter-related bloodstream infections (CRBSI). The Guideline Development Group (GDG) concluded that chlorhexidine-containing products may have small desirable effects and potentially moderate undesirable effects, but there was no significant variability in patient preferences regarding the most critical outcomes. As a result, the GDG determined that either chlorhexidine-containing or non-chlorhexidine-containing skin disinfection products could be used before catheter insertion in these populations, as there was insufficient evidence to recommend one over the other. Some GDG members noted that alcohol-chlorhexidine combinations, particularly 2% chlorhexidine, are generally considered superior to chlorhexidine alone or alcohol alone. These combinations may also be associated with a lower risk of peripheral intravenous catheter (PIVC) colonization by potential pathogens compared to alcohol-povidone-iodine preparations. A review of the literature identified nine studies (seven randomized controlled trials [RCTs] and two non-randomized studies of interventions [NRSIs]) comparing chlorhexidine-containing skin disinfection products to non-chlorhexidine-containing products in adults, adolescents, children, and neonates. Seven studies focused on PIVC, and two on peripherally inserted central catheters (PICC). These studies included data from 4,491 patients across Canada, France, Iran, Japan, Thailand, and the USA. Two RCTs were rated as having a high risk of bias, four with some concerns, and one with a low risk of bias. All NRSIs were rated as having some risk of bias concerns. No study reported on bloodstream infection (BSI)-related mortality, sepsis, or all-cause mortality. For PICC insertion in adults, children, and neonates, the evidence was very uncertain regarding the effect of chlorhexidine-containing skin disinfection compared to non-chlorhexidine-containing products on CRBSI. One cohort study reported an increased risk of CRBSI with less than 1% chlorhexidine compared to 10% povidone-iodine, but no statistically significant difference was observed when using more than 1% chlorhexidine. No study reported on BSI-related mortality, sepsis, local infections, or phlebitis/thrombophlebitis. The GDG emphasized the importance of formal training for healthcare workers (HCWs) performing catheter insertions. Formal training was deemed essential for PICC and peripherally inserted arterial catheter (PAC) insertions and important for PIVC insertions in adults, adolescents, and children. For neonates, formal training was considered critical for all catheter types due to the challenges associated with insertion in this population. The evidence suggested that formal training reduces complications such as phlebitis and insertion-related issues, although the certainty of evidence was very low. The GDG also recommended that clinicians inserting PIVCs or PICCs wear single-use gloves during the procedure. However, for neonates, where tactile agility is crucial, clinicians may have the option to forego gloves if appropriate hand hygiene is performed. This recommendation was based on the balance of moderate desirable effects and small undesirable effects, with no significant variability in patient preferences. Implementation of formal training programs should include both theoretical education and practical competency demonstrations. Training should be sustainable, involve all stakeholders, and consider local contexts and resources. Simulation tools may be beneficial but could be less accessible in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) due to cost constraints. Research is needed to identify the most time-efficient and effective methods for catheter insertion training and skill retention, particularly in resource-limited settings.
